In managed lands around the world, the connections among soil, vegetation, water, climate, and human decisions are visible in the landscape. Change in one part of the system is rarely contained there. Its effects travel across watersheds, across livelihood systems and increasingly across national borders. Those who work on the land also learn a second lesson. Good decisions depend on observations over time. A single measurement can be informative but is rarely sufficient. We need consistent methods, trusted data, local knowledge, and the patience to understand change before we can respond effectively. Experience has also shown that information becomes valuable only when it can be interpreted and used by people responsible for managing land. These lessons are highly relevant to the work before us. During this session, we must connect global assessments with national circumstances. scientific knowledge with practical experience, technological innovation with institutional capacity, and long-term ambition with decisions that can be acted upon now. Our agenda gives us several opportunities to do so. The proposed land stewardship framing asks us to look beyond land management as a collection of technical interventions. It invites us to consider how societies understand and value land, how institutions and incentives shape decisions, and how practices are adapted to the realities of particular landscapes. That framing resonates with a fundamental feature of land systems. There is no universal prescription. A measure that succeeds in one place may fail in another because soils, climate, tenure arrangements, livelihoods, or institutional capacities differ. Scientific guidance must therefore be rigorous without becoming detached from context. It must identify general principles while leaving room for locally adapted solutions. We will also have the opportunity to discuss the interconnections among land, water, food, health and climate. Sustainable land management, restoration, water management, and drought resilience can reinforce one another, particularly when they are designed together at appropriate scales and with attention to possible trade-offs. The agenda item on aridity and drought offers a practical example. Aridity and drought are related, but they are not the same. Effective planning requires us to understand both long-term changes in water availability and shorter-term drought events, and to connect that understanding with national planning instruments. Our discussions on knowledge sharing and innovation raise another practical question. How do we ensure that knowledge reaches those who need it? Digital platforms, earth observation, modelling and artificial intelligence create significant possibilities. Yet technology alone does not close a knowledge gap. Tools must be transparent, accessible, appropriate to national circumstances and supported by the capacity to use and interpret them. The same principle applies to reporting. Comparable global information is essential, but so is national ownership. The strongest monitoring systems are those in which common standards and country-specific data complement one another. grounded in an understanding of land potential. Our joint discussion with the CRIC should therefore help us consider not only the quality of reported data, but also how reporting can serve planning, learning, and decision-making within countries. Agricultural lands and soils will be another major focus. Here, the land degradation neutrality response hierarchy provides a disciplined starting point. First, avoid degradation, then reduce ongoing degradation, and reverse past degradation where necessary and achievable. This sequence matters. Restoration cannot substitute indefinitely for preventing avoidable damage. In croplands and rangelands alike, prevention is often more effective, less costly, and more durable. Finally, we have the opportunity to consider the future functioning of the science policy interface. The question is not simply what structure we establish, but what kind of scientific evidence parties need. Thank you, Mr. Chair, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, ladies and gentlemen. It's my honor to present the synthesis report today. The guide is structured in three parts. Part one provides the rationale for synergistic approach to aridity and drought adaptation across the Rio Conventions and the Sendai Framework. Part two is a practical guide on how to plan for aridity and drought adaptation at national level. Part three presents case studies from different regions that illustrate best practices and lessons learned to inspire action. The structure of this presentation follows these parts and presents the key findings and key messages. The first key message is that aridity and drought risks are systemic. Observations of past and current impacts together with future projections show that aridity and drought have far-reaching impacts. Diminishing water availability and the drying of soils drive ecosystem deterioration, biodiversity loss and compound hazards such as wildfires and sand and dust storms. And land degradation can reinforce adverse climate feedback loops. They also exacerbate water and food insecurity for millions of people worldwide, put multiple sectors and systems under stress, and may also contribute to competition over increasingly scarce resources. As aridity and drought impacts affect people differently depending on gender, age, disability, livelihood, income, ethnicity, and social status, they also increase social vulnerability and inequality. Because they are embedded in complex interconnected systems, these risks are systemic. Addressing interconnected aridity and drought risks and impacts and the challenges that arise from them require holistic, comprehensive risk management approaches. Such approaches often require collaboration and coordinated action at multiple governance levels across sectors, borders and policy domains. This can be achieved by building on the synergies among the goals and targets of relevant multilateral environmental agreements and international frameworks, such as the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification, the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, the Convention on Biological Diversity, and the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction. These conventions and frameworks with their global goals can guide planning for aridity and drought adaptation, while adaptation outcomes in turn support the achievement of multiple global goals. This guide focuses on realizing synergies that can help bridge gaps between convention and framework specific objectives and adaptation planning processes at global and national level. Here, planning instruments are levers for synergies. Relevant national planning instruments include land degradation neutrality target setting, national drought plans, national adaptation plans, national biodiversity strategies and action plans, and disaster risk reduction strategies. They provide key entry points to integrate aridity and drought adaptation and to harness synergies among the framework's goals and targets across sectors and governance levels, reduce siloed approaches and strengthen resilience. The legal and policy foundations to facilitate synergies for aridity and drought adaptation are embedded in the foundational convention text and frameworks, An overview of the respective articles is provided in the report. The integration across the multiple national planning instruments of the Rio Conventions and the Sendai Framework began with a systematic comparison of the various steps, elements and modules outlined in the technical guidelines for each instrument to identify core components that enable synergistic adaptation. This is schematically shown on this slide. This comparison identified the principal similarities of these instruments and subsequently clustered them into seven components forming the backbone of this guide and which are detailed in part two of the guide. Each of these components is refined to provide more detailed action points to more effectively direct aridity and drought adaptation for countries. The instruments share core components for synergistic adaptation to aridity and drought, which include strengthening enabling conditions, inclusive and comprehensive risk assessment and management, alignment of national targets with global goals, selection and prioritization of robust adaptation actions, and coherent monitoring, evaluation, learning, and reporting supported by adequate and accessible finance. Integrating aridity and drought into these shared components can make adaptation more effective and can usefully leverage existing planning cycles and coordinating mechanisms. To ensure that adaptation is both effective and equitable, these processes should consider how aridity and drought affect different population groups and whether adaptation measures reach and benefit those that are most exposed to risk. Each component of the practical guide provides detailed guidance together with the underlying scientific evidence and policy rationale. It is important to say that the components and action points are intended as entry points for identifying and realizing synergies across planning processes rather than an alternative set of planning actions. Realizing the potential synergies identified in the guide requires coordinated action at global, national, and local levels. Coordinated action includes enhanced collaboration, data and information sharing, and financing mechanisms across national ministries, technical agencies, local governments, the private sector, and civil society. Within countries, bridging national planning instruments and processes under these frameworks depends on deliberate coordination to avoid fragmented or conflicting interventions, reduce transaction costs, and leverage additional resources. At the global level, the secretariats and partner institutions can add value by aligning guidance, technical support, and monitoring systems around shared objectives on aridity and drought and other cross-cutting challenges. These findings have several practical implications. These include improving institutional and governance arrangements to overcome siloed decision-making and implementation of adaptation strategies. and promoting the meaningful participation of affected communities, including women, indigenous people and local communities, persons with disabilities and other underrepresented groups. Investing in science and data to underpin comprehensive risk assessment and management for aridity and drought risks, such as through early warning systems, as well as sectoral climate services. This includes using sex, age, disability, disaggregated data and local knowledge where available. Prioritizing sustainable land management, integrated water resource management and practices, nature-based solutions and integrated land use planning that deliver multiple benefits across environmental, economic and social dimensions. And finally, mobilizing and streamlining finance, including innovative mechanisms and blended finance structures to sustain proactive risk reduction and long-term adaptation efforts, and improving access to adaptation resources for groups that often face barriers to finance and support services. Part three of the report presents case studies from different regions that illustrate such examples from research and practice, and reflect on each of the components of part two. They provide good practices, lessons learned, challenges and opportunities for aridity and drought adaptation and highlight potential synergies across the Rio Conventions and the Sendai Framework to inspire planning in other countries. Examples of the insights of these case studies are highlighted and listed on this slide. They include, for example, how community participate in drought risk assessments and water stewardship for climate adaptation, biodiversity and disaster risk reduction, or how anticipatory funding in action strengthens adaptive capacities to drought. The challenge now is not to invent a new agenda, but to connect the ones that we already have. This means finding ways for existing efforts to work across goals rather than in isolation. As countries strengthen now their efforts to address the growing challenges of aridity and drought, there is an increased need for planning approaches that are coherent, coordinated and mutually enforcing. And we see that there is a growing potential to move forward toward more coordinated and where appropriate, joint planning and implementation across land, climate, biodiversity and disaster risk reduction. It is now time to build on existing synergies, strengthen partnerships, and join forces to create more resilient landscapes, communities, and economies in the decades ahead. With this, I conclude the presentation and thank you.
